overview: Netwealth is an ASX-listed, Melbourne-founded wealth management technology company that operates an investor-directed portfolio service (IDPS/wrap) platform, a superannuation master fund and managed account infrastructure used by financial advisers and their retail, high-net-worth and institutional clients across Australia. Revenue is earned primarily as basis-point fees on Funds Under Administration (FUA, $135.7bn at FY26) and Funds Under Management (FUM, $34.6bn), supplemented by cash, transaction, brokerage and foreign-exchange related fees. The company is one of two dominant independent 'specialist' platforms (alongside HUB24) that have taken sustained share from legacy bank-owned and insurer platforms (BT Panorama, Macquarie Wrap, CFS, MLC/IOOF) over the past decade.

business_model.summary: Netwealth charges administration/platform fees (basis points on FUA, with tiering and caps on larger balances), cash margin/transaction fees on pooled cash balances, management fees on its own managed account and managed fund products (FUM), and ancillary fees from brokerage, custody and FX. The model is highly operationally geared: revenue scales with asset balances and account growth while the core technology cost base is largely fixed, so incremental FUA/FUM growth drives EBITDA margin expansion over time (ex one-off items).

revenue_streams.name: Cash fees (margin on pooled cash balances)
Transaction, brokerage, FX and ancillary fees

business_model.customer_type: B2B2C — distributed via ~4,200 financial intermediaries (advisers/licensees) to retail, high-net-worth, SMSF and a smaller institutional/stockbroking client base; revenue is recurring (basis-point fee on sticky invested balances) rather than transactional or project-based
business_model.geographic_mix: Almost entirely Australia-domestic; platform revenue/average FUA of ~30.7bps in FY26; FUA $135.7bn, FUM $34.6bn, 182,276 accounts, 4,205 financial intermediaries at FY26

competitive_position.market_position: One of the two leading independent 'next-generation' wrap platforms in Australia; grew FUA market share to 9.7% in FY26 (+98bps), and has been taking share from bank-owned legacy platforms for over a decade. HUB24 has recently grown its market share faster and overtaken or matched Netwealth in platform FUA, making this an intense, duopolistic rivalry that is widely seen as capping pricing power for both players.

moat_factors.description: Advisers and licensees build practice workflows, managed account models and client reporting around a single platform; migrating FUA is costly and disruptive, creating adviser stickiness once onboarded
Fixed technology cost base means growing FUA/FUM drives operating leverage; FY27 EBITDA margin guided to ~47% ex one-offs, among the highest in the sector
Consistently top-ranked by advisers for platform functionality and service in adviser-technology surveys, supporting continued net inflows and intermediary growth
4,205 financial intermediaries and growing managed-account menu attract more advisers and fund managers in a reinforcing loop

Platform/custodian licensing creates some barrier to new entrants, but it has not prevented well-capitalised competitors (HUB24, bank platforms) from competing aggressively, and the First Guardian episode shows licensing comes with material governance/liability obligations rather than pure protection

weaknesses: Intense two-horse-race dynamic with HUB24 constrains pricing and requires continuous reinvestment in features
Platform revenue/average FUA margin has been gradually declining (31.5bps FY25 to 30.7bps FY26) due to fee caps/tiering on larger accounts
Reliance on a 'gatekeeper' role for investment options exposed Netwealth to First Guardian-style fund-manager failure risk despite not managing the failed fund itself
Single-market (Australia) concentration with no meaningful geographic diversification
Reputational and governance damage from First Guardian could weigh on new adviser/licensee wins in the near term

growth_drivers: Explicit management ambition to double FUA over four years to FY30 ('Dx30'), underpinned by market share gains, adviser-led growth and operating leverage
Launch of Netwealth Private for high-net-worth/ultra-high-net-worth clients, bringing wholesale funds, private markets, bonds, structured products and derivatives onto the platform
Entry into stockbroking/individual HIN and ASX-listed securities administration (new ~$600bn addressable market), anchored by an expanded Morgan Stanley Wealth Management Australia relationship
Continued managed account penetration (FUM +27.9% to $34.6bn in FY26; managed accounts +29.9% to $30.5bn) as advisers outsource portfolio construction

Acquisition of Paradino (AI-enabled adviser workflow platform, announced Sept 2026, up to ~A$29-39m total consideration) extending Netwealth's addressable role across the adviser workflow (advice generation, file notes, records of advice), not just platform administration
AI investment across the platform (NOVA client/adviser assistant, AI development tooling, Snowflake cloud migration) aimed at adviser productivity and platform scalability
Structural secular tailwind: ongoing shift of FUA from legacy bank/insurer platforms to independent specialist platforms, plus generational wealth transfer and growing superannuation pool

business.description: HUB24's market share has grown faster recently; duopolistic competition pressures fees and requires continual feature investment
As a platform offering thousands of investment options, Netwealth is exposed to failures of underlying fund managers (as with First Guardian) even without directly managing the failed assets
Platform revenue/average FUA has declined for two consecutive years (31.5bps to 30.7bps) due to tiered/capped fees on larger balances

business.risk: Execution risk on new growth initiatives
business.description: Netwealth Private, individual HIN/broking and the Paradino acquisition are unproven expansions into adjacent markets

financial.risk: First Guardian cash and earnings impact
financial.description: A$100.7m compensation payment plus A$4.5m costs drove a 1H26 statutory net loss and cut FY26 statutory NPAT to A$60.7m (vs adjusted A$135.4m); NTA per share fell from 70.7c to 52.5c
Total debt appeared on balance sheet in FY26 (A$58.3m) for the first time in the company's recent history, alongside lease/other liabilities rising
FY26 dividends paid exceeded statutory NPAT due to FG expenses; company intends to base dividends on underlying (ex-FG) earnings, but policy execution should be monitored

regulatory.description: Netwealth Superannuation Services is under an APRA enforceable undertaking requiring a multi-year overhaul of investment governance, with independent oversight; execution risk and ongoing compliance cost

In August 2026 the Federal Court declared Netwealth Superannuation Services and Netwealth Investments contravened the Corporations Act over First Guardian (no pecuniary penalty imposed given cooperation and full compensation), raising the bar for super-fund gatekeeper due diligence industry-wide

A class action was lodged in September 2026 against Netwealth Investments and Netwealth Superannuation Services related to First Guardian, despite the ~A$101m compensation already paid; quantum and timing of any further liability is unresolved

ASIC is pursuing related proceedings against other trustees/platforms (Macquarie/Shield, Equity Trustees, Diversa) over similar managed investment scheme failures, signalling a sector-wide tightening of gatekeeper obligations that will raise industry compliance costs

macro.description: FUA market movement contributed materially to growth in prior years; a sustained equity market downturn would reduce average balances, fee revenue and reported FUA/FUM growth

macro.risk: Interest rate sensitivity on cash margin
macro.description: Cash fee revenue depends on pooled cash balances and the margin earned; falling interest rates would compress this revenue stream
Platform growth depends on the number and productivity of financial advisers in Australia, a sector that has seen headcount declines post Royal Commission, though stabilising

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Australian retail wealth platform/administration market continues to grow via superannuation guarantee inflows, compulsory super balances, and ongoing migration of FUA from legacy bank/insurer platforms to independent specialist platforms (Netwealth, HUB24); industry commentary expects competition to intensify specifically between Netwealth and HUB24
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate — revenue is largely balance-based (bps on FUA/FUM) so it correlates with equity/bond market levels and net inflows, but recurring administration fees provide some defensiveness versus purely transactional businesses
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate — cash fee revenue (margin on pooled transaction account balances, ~5.8% of custodial FUA) is directly exposed to RBA cash rate moves and deposit margins
key_input_costs: Regulatory compliance/legal costs (elevated post-First Guardian/Program RISE)

recent_developments.event: Netwealth reached agreement with ASIC and entered an enforceable undertaking with APRA, agreeing to compensate First Guardian-affected Netwealth Superannuation Master Fund members in full (~A$100.7m paid into accounts by 30 January 2026); admitted contraventions of the Corporations Act
H1 FY2026 results: statutory net loss of A$2.2m (vs A$57.6m profit pcp) due to A$101.7m First Guardian expenses; adjusted (ex-FG) NPAT of A$69.0m, up 19.9% on pcp; FUA reached a record A$125.6bn

Federal Court (ASIC v Netwealth Investments Limited [2026] FCA 1186) declared Netwealth Superannuation Services and Netwealth Investments contravened the Corporations Act in relation to First Guardian; no pecuniary penalty sought given cooperation and completed compensation; Netwealth ordered to pay ASIC's costs

FY2026 full-year results: record FUA of A$135.7bn (+20.3%), FUM A$34.6bn (+27.9%), adjusted EBITDA A$191.5-192.9m (+18%), adjusted NPAT A$135.4m (+16.2%); statutory NPAT of A$60.7m after A$105.2m total First Guardian expenses; launched Netwealth Private and announced Dx30 (double FUA by FY30) ambition; FY27 guidance of A$18-20bn net flows and ~47% EBITDA margin ex FG/RISE expenses

Announced acquisition of Scale Up Platform Solutions (trading as Paradino), an AI-enabled adviser workflow platform, for up to ~A$29-39m total consideration including earn-outs and planned follow-on investment

Disclosed a class action lodged against Netwealth Investments Limited and Netwealth Superannuation Services Pty Ltd relating to First Guardian investment options, despite prior full compensation; shares fell sharply (reported 6-8% single-day drop) and traded near two-year lows amid the news flow

items.notes: FY26 net flows were $15.4bn; guidance implies continued acceleration
Explicitly excludes First Guardian expenses and Program RISE project expenses; FY26 adjusted EBITDA margin (ex-FG) was ~49.3% of total income, so this may imply margin give-back from RISE investment
Relates to platform/product technology capitalisation, excludes Paradino-related investment

Supported by market share gains, adviser productivity, product innovation (Netwealth Private, HIN/broking, Paradino) and operating leverage; not a formal earnings guidance figure but a stated long-term objective

items.target: No material impact on near-term earnings; Paradino expected EBITDA loss of ~A$3 million
items.notes: Management stated existing FY27 guidance is maintained on a pre-acquisition basis

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Matt Heine and the Board characterised FY26 as a year of record operating growth (FUA, FUM, accounts, intermediaries) overshadowed by the First Guardian matter, describing the response (compensation, APRA enforceable undertaking, Program RISE investment governance overhaul) as the Board's foremost priority. Management reiterated confidence in long-term structural tailwinds (shift to specialist platforms, adviser productivity, managed accounts) and said the balance sheet remains strong with high recurring revenue and robust cash generation to fund the Dx30 ambition despite the FG cash outflow.

bull_case: Core platform economics remain excellent: record FUA/FUM growth, rising adviser/account numbers, and adjusted (ex-FG) NPAT and EPS both up ~16% in FY26, with FY27 EBITDA margin guided to ~47%

First Guardian liability appears largely resolved from a cash perspective (compensation already paid, no ASIC penalty imposed), removing the biggest near-term tail risk even as reputational and class-action risk linger
Structural secular tailwind of FUA migrating from legacy bank/insurer platforms to independent specialist platforms continues to favour Netwealth and HUB24 as the clear share winners

Credible, funded expansion into adjacent markets (Netwealth Private, HIN/stockbroking via Morgan Stanley relationship, AI-enabled adviser workflow via Paradino) broadens the addressable market well beyond core platform administration and underpins the Dx30 (double FUA by FY30) ambition

Sell-off following First Guardian/class-action news (shares reportedly down ~30-40% from highs, trading near multi-year lows) may have overcorrected relative to the still-growing, high-margin, recurring-revenue core business, creating a valuation entry point if governance risk is now priced in
bear_case: First Guardian is not fully closed out: a new class action (filed September 2026) creates open-ended, unquantified additional liability risk on top of the ~A$101m already paid, and the Federal Court's contravention findings set an adverse legal precedent for platform/trustee due diligence obligations

APRA's enforceable undertaking and Program RISE impose a multi-year, costly governance overhaul with execution risk and ongoing compliance drag on margins, with management itself flagging RISE expenses as a drag on FY27 EBITDA margin guidance

Intensifying duopolistic competition with HUB24, which has been taking market share at a faster rate recently, pressures fee margins (platform revenue/average FUA already declined for two straight years) and demands continuous reinvestment
Reputational damage from First Guardian could slow new adviser/licensee acquisition and dent the trust-based 'gatekeeper' value proposition that underpins the platform's pricing power

Valuation has historically been rich (growth-platform multiple); any slowdown in net flows, further litigation costs, or macro-driven market declines (which reduce average FUA/FUM) could compress both earnings and the multiple simultaneously
